           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                    )
          OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                      ) Case No. PUD2026-000031
          FOR COMMISSION APPROVAL OF ELECTRIC                    )
          SERVICE AGREEMENTS AND PREAPPROVAL                     )
          OF CAPACITY PURCHASE AGREEMENTS                        )
          PURSUANT TO 17 O.S. § 286(C)                           )




                                            Rebuttal Testimony

                                                     of

                                             Kimber L. Shoop

                                                 on behalf of

                                    Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company

         Rebuttal Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                  Page 1 of 8

                                                Kimber L. Shoop
                                               Rebuttal Testimony

    1    Q.    Please state your name and business address.
    2    A.    My name is Kimber L. Shoop. My business address is 321 North Harvey, Oklahoma City,
    3          Oklahoma 73102.
    4
    5    Q.    Are you the same Kimber L. Shoop who filed Direct Testimony in this case on May 1,
    6          2026?
    7    A.    Yes, I am.
    8
    9    Q.    What is the purpose of your testimony?
   10    A.    The purpose of my testimony is to summarize the case up to this point, and to respond to a
   11          few of the arguments raised in Responsive Testimony.
   12
   13    Q.    Please summarize the Responsive Testimony and the parties’ positions in the case up
   14          to this point.
   15    A.    All parties in the case are generally supportive of the ESAs and the CPAs that OG&E
   16          requested approval for in its Application. All witnesses appear to agree on the following:
   17              •   OG&E has a capacity need;
   18              •   The CPAs are reasonably priced and appear favorable to market alternatives;
   19              •   The ESAs contain substantial customer protections;
   20              •   Existing customers are likely to benefit, or at a minimum, are protected from harm;
   21                  and
   22              •   Approval is generally appropriate.

   23          OG&E is appreciative of the supportive response from intervenors in this case and I believe
   24          it is a testament to the many months OG&E dedicated to finding a way to serve Google
   25          while ensuring that existing customers do not see any negative impacts. There are just a
   26          few issues that need to be addressed in Rebuttal Testimony.
   27
   28    Q.    Who is filing Rebuttal Testimony for OG&E?
   29    A.    OG&E witness Thenmadathil is filing Rebuttal Testimony regarding the calculation of
   30          potential benefit of adding the Google load to the OG&E system, PUD’s recommendation

         Rebuttal Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                Page 2 of 8
         Case No. PUD2026-000031

    1          regarding the annual review and offsetting regulatory asset and liability, and future
    2          customer impact reviews. OG&E witness Schuermann is filing Rebuttal Testimony
    3          regarding reasonable alternatives and the acquisition of capacity outside of an RFP.
    4          Finally, my Rebuttal Testimony will discuss reasonable alternatives, and various intervenor
    5          recommendations regarding additional customer protections and annual reviews.
    6
    7    Q.    Please describe your understanding of 17 O.S. § 286(C), also known as “the pre-
    8          approval statute.”
    9    A.    The pre-approval statute allows rate-regulated electric companies like OG&E to file an
   10          application seeking Commission approval “to construct a new electric generating facility,
   11          to purchase an existing electric generating facility or enter into a long-term contract for
   12          purchased power and capacity and/or energy.”
   13                 The statute further states that “[i]f, and to the extent that, the Commission
   14          determines there is a need for construction or purchase of the electric generating facility or
   15          long-term purchase power contract, the generating facility or contract shall be considered
   16          used and useful and its costs shall be subject to cost recovery rules promulgated by the
   17          Commission.” This means that to satisfy the requirements of the statute, OG&E must show
   18          there is a need and, if OG&E can show a facility is needed, then such facility is considered
   19          used and useful, and subject to cost recovery.
   20                 Finally, the statute says that the Commission shall enter an order in the pre-approval
   21          case “after consideration of reasonable alternatives.” This requires there to be evidence of
   22          consideration of reasonable alternatives presented to the Commission during the pendency
   23          of the proceeding.
   24
   25    Q.    Has OG&E complied with the requirements of 17 O.S. § 286(C)?
   26    A.    Yes. Based upon OG&E’s Integrated Resource Plans, OG&E has established that it has a
   27          need for new generating capacity. No party in this proceeding disputes that OG&E has a
   28          need for the capacity. Additionally, based on the comparison performed by our resource
   29          planning team and as testified by OG&E witness Schuermann, OG&E also considered
   30          reasonable alternatives. Therefore, OG&E has satisfied the requirements of 17 O.S. §



         Rebuttal Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                   Page 3 of 8
         Case No. PUD2026-000031
 CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 105 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/21/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 9




    1          286(C) and recommends approval of the Rush Springs and High Spring Capacity Purchase
    2          Agreements (“CPAs”).
    3
    4                                  REASONABLE ALTERNATIVES
    5    Q.    PUD witness Givens raises questions regarding the consideration of reasonable
    6          alternatives for the CPAs because they were not bid into an RFP, and “only grant
    7          preapproval if it finds that evaluation of reasonable alternatives was impossible…”1
    8          How do you respond?
    9    A.    This argument is confusing to me for a couple of reasons. First, there is nothing in the pre-
   10          approval statute or in the OCC rules that require a capacity resource to be bid into an RFP
   11          in order to demonstrate that reasonable alternatives have been considered. Section 286(C)
   12          does not require competitive bidding in order to demonstrate a consideration of reasonable
   13          alternatives.    If the legislature intended to require a competitive solicitation as
   14          “consideration of reasonable alternatives,” it would have said so. The Legislature clearly
   15          knows how to mandate competitive solicitations because it did so in Section 286(C)(7)
   16          when it required electric utilities to conduct competitive solicitations for contracts to
   17          transport natural gas to any generating facility approved for construction under Section
   18          286(C). Importantly, the Commission’s rules that implement Section 286(C) are quite
   19          clear that competitive bidding is not required. Those rules state, “[a] case shall be opened
   20          by the utility for cost recovery if the competitive bidding RFP process established in
   21          165:35-34 is not utilized and the utility wishes to gain approval of cost before construction
   22          starts.” See OAC 165:35-38-5(e) (“Self-Build or Purchase Options”).
   23                  The important thing is that there is an assessment of what generation capacity is
   24          currently available and how a chosen project compares to those available alternatives. In
   25          this case, OG&E recently conducted an RFP and assessed the market for new generation
   26          capacity and then compared the CPAs requested for approval in this case to that recent
   27          RFP. That RFP constitutes extremely clear and timely evidence of what is available in the
   28          market as an alternative to the CPAs. Second, a recent amendment to the pre-approval
   29          statute expressly allows offers to be compared to competitive solicitations within 12
   30          months of receiving bids. Section 286(C)(2) specifically states: “Bids received by the

    1          utility through a competitive bidding process within the twelve (12) months following the
    2          final bid due date of such competitive bidding process shall be considered substantial
    3          evidence to satisfy the consideration of reasonable alternatives.”2
    4
    5    Q.    Did OG&E receive the CPA offers within 12 months of receiving bids from its 2024
    6          All Source RFP?
    7    A.    Yes, it did. OG&E received bids in its 2024 All Source RFP on September 25, 2024, and
    8          the CPAs were offered well before September 2025. Final pricing was established with
    9          the CPAs on September 12, 2025. Therefore, by comparing the CPAs to the bids received
   10          in the 2024 All Source RFP, OG&E statutorily meets the pre-approval requirement to
   11          demonstrate it appropriately considered reasonable alternatives.
   12
   13    Q.    As requested by PUD, do you believe that the Commission should set an “intentionally
   14          high bar to discourage utilities from evading RFP requirements…”?3
   15    A.    No. As described above, there are no RFP requirements and OG&E is in no way evading
   16          RFP requirements. I believe PUD’s characterization is unfair, and it ignores the reality of
   17          the market we are in today, the statute, and Commission rules. OG&E has a tremendous
   18          need and may need to look beyond bids received in an RFP for its capacity solutions. As
   19          long as the Company assesses reasonable alternatives when seeking preapproval, the test
   20          for prudence should remain the same: is the project fair, just, reasonable, and in the public
   21          interest? There should not be some higher unknown burden adopted in this Case for
   22          projects that are clearly reasonable just because they came to the Company outside of an
   23          RFP.
   24                  For all the reasons I discuss above, OG&E met the statutory requirements for pre-
   25          approval with regard to these CPAs.        There is nothing that requires a competitive
   26          solicitation to be the only basis for a comparison of reasonable alternatives. OG&E does
   27          issue RFPs when it has capacity needs and follows the Commission’s competitive bidding
   28          rules. Sometimes there are circumstances that require the acquisition of capacity outside
   29          of an RFP, such as in cases where the bids in an RFP are simply not enough capacity or do

               17 O.S. § 286(C)(2) (OSCN 2026).
         3

    1          not provide it quickly enough to satisfy capacity needs. The current instance is a great
    2          example of how arrangements outside of an RFP can be even more beneficial to customers
    3          than bids from inside the RFP.
    4                  Regardless, the Commission’s evaluation of a utility’s evaluation of reasonable
    5          alternatives for purposes of a review pursuant to Section 286(C) is not limited to an RFP
    6          and PUD’s position that the Commission should only grant preapproval if it finds that
    7          evaluation of reasonable alternatives was impossible is not supported by rule or statute. In
    8          fact, OG&E has provided substantial evaluation of the market, the CPAs, and reasonable
    9          alternatives to the CPAs.
   10
   11                                           FAIL SAFE PROVISION
   12    Q.    What have some of the responsive witnesses said about the failsafe provision
   13          identified in the Google Electric Service Agreements (“ESAs”)?
   14    A.    PUD and AG witnesses discuss some of their specific proposals about how the “fail safe”
   15          provision should operate. For example, PUD Witness Givens recommends that OG&E
   16          perform the “with and without” Google analysis every year, but not in the annual fuel
   17          review.4 AG Witness Beling outlines very specific details on how the “with and without
   18          Google” analysis should be done.5
   19                  In the XLPL Tariff proceeding in Case No. PUD2026-00046, OG&E has proposed
   20          a Customer Class Protection Charge to embody the “fail safe” concept. The details of that
   21          calculation and the “with and without” analysis of the XLPL load will be decided by the
   22          Commission in a general rate case following the addition of the XLPL load to the system
   23          and after OG&E has the details of the costs to serve those new customers. When that
   24          general rate case occurs, OG&E will propose a plan to perform that “with and without”
   25          analysis and collaborate with intervening parties to ensure it is done in the most reasonable
   26          and fairest way possible for all customers. OG&E believes it is premature for the
   27          Commission to determine precisely how that analysis should be done until it has all
   28          relevant facts and circumstances to be able to make an informed decision.




         4
               Givens Responsive, 19:12–20:5.
         5
               Beling Responsive, 23–27.

    1                                          CONCLUSION
    2    Q.    What are your recommendations to the Commission?
    3    A.    OG&E is requesting the Commission grant approval of its three Electric Service
    4          Agreements with Google and pre-approval of the two CPAs requested herein pursuant to
    5          17 O.S. § 286(C). With regard to the CPAs, OG&E requests that the Commission make a
    6          determination that OG&E has a need for the capacity provided by these CPAs and that the
    7          CPAs are reasonable compared to the All-Source RFP bids. These CPAs represent the
    8          lowest reasonable cost options for meeting OG&E’s current resource capacity needs.
    9                 The Company also requests the Commission authorize OG&E to recover the costs
   10          of the CPAs through its FCA, similar to the recovery granted for OG&E’s CPAs approved
   11          in Case No. PUD2025-000038.
   12                 The record demonstrates that OG&E has a capacity need, has considered reasonable
   13          alternatives, and has negotiated customer protections that multiple responsive witnesses
   14          acknowledge are substantial and effective. Remaining disputes largely involve future rate
   15          design and future regulatory frameworks. Those matters will be addressed in future rate
   16          cases without delaying approval of the ESAs and CPAs that provide immediate economic
   17          development benefits, incremental capacity resources, and protections for existing
   18          customers.
   19
   20    Q.    Does your testimony address all issues raised by parties in their responsive testimony?
   21    A.    No. My Rebuttal Testimony is limited in scope and does not address all issues raised in
   22          this proceeding. My silence on any issue should not be construed as agreement with
   23          another party’s testimony.
   24
   25    Q.    Does this conclude your testimony?
   26    A.    Yes.
